newsitem.title: UK: Moscow Eurobond plans spark talk of maturity curbs.
newsitem.headline: Moscow Eurobond plans spark talk of maturity curbs.

text.p: Plans for Moscow's debut Eurobond, due in May and set to have a three-year maturity, raised speculation in the Eurobond market other Russian municipalities could also be restricted to short-dated issues, London bankers said on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, a source in the City of Moscow government said the city had registered a $400 million three-year Eurobond. It had been previously thought that Moscow might issue a five-year Eurobond.
Russian borrowers need authorisation to issue Eurobonds from a number of entities, including the ministry of finance and the central bank, bankers said.
Bankers said a central bank licence granted for Moscow's Eurobond expired after three years, constraining the maturity of the bond.

"When the central bank licence is issued it has an expiration date on it, and this will limit your flexibility in accessing the capital markets," a banker familiar with Moscow's Eurobond preparations said.
"If the license expires in three years you can't do a deal that is longer than three years," he said.
Bankers specialising in Russia said it was unclear whether the constraint applied to Moscow specifically, or whether it would affect planned bonds from St Petersburg and the Nizhny Novgorod region.

"All we have heard is Moscow's deal will have a three-year maturity, but we have not heard anything which would suggest that this is the limit for other borrowers," a banker involved with one of the other Russian municipalities said.
"We would not rule it out, but we have not heard anything to that effect," he said.
Another Russian specialist said he would be surprised if other municipalities were given permission for longer-dated bonds.

"I can't imagine that the central bank will give the capital city, with the most political clout, one licence and other cities a licence which gives them more freedom. Moscow will be the benchmark," he said.

Moscow would be the first non-sovereign Russian borrower to issue an international bond. So far, only the government has raised money abroad, via a $1.0 billion five-year bond and a 2.0 billion mark seven-year deal.
The authorisation process for municipality bond issues remain murky, bankers said.
"At this point there is no indication from any authority of a maturity constraint," a banker said.

"But you need to be very careful what you apply for in Russia. You have to consider very carefully what questions you ask, as the bureaucracy does not provide a flexible response. Moscow may be restrained to a three-year maturity because of the questions asked," he said.
Credit Suisse First Boston and Nomura will be joint lead managers for Moscow's transaction, but officials there declined to comment on terms for the deal.
Moscow will hold a series of roadshows in Asia, Europe and the U.S. between May 12 and May 23. Its Eurobond could be launched shortly after, bankers said.
